## Priority genes for natural variation in Arabidopsis seed dormancy

**1. DOG1 (AT5G45830) — top priority.** The strongest case for both genetic and functional evidence. It was positionally cloned as a dormancy QTL [1](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0607877103) and is reported to be required for the induction of seed dormancy [1](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0607877103); dog1 loss-of-function seeds are non-dormant [2](https://doi.org/10.1111/pce.12940)[3](https://doi.org/10.1093/jxb/erac150). Natural variation is documented at the locus itself: a series of functionally distinct alleles segregate at DOG1, and differentiation patterns support its contribution to local adaptation [4](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1558-5646.2012.01590.x); allelic variants are associated with natural variation in primary dormancy, after-ripening and field germination timing [5](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1912451117). Mechanistically, natural allelic variation in the DOG1 promoter affects bZIP67-dependent transactivation, linking ecotypic dormancy differences to a defined regulatory interaction [6](https://doi.org/10.1105/tpc.18.00892), and DOG1 expression tracks seed-maturation temperature and geography [7](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-294x.2011.05181.x).

**2. RDO5/DOG18 (AT4G11040) — second priority.** A dormancy QTL (DOG18) that is the same gene as RDO5, a clade-A PP2C-family pseudophosphatase [8](https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.16.00525). Natural loss-of-function alleles occur at relatively high frequency in northwestern European accessions and reduce dormancy, and their effect can be compensated by DOG1 and DOG6 and by low temperature [8](https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.16.00525). Mutant evidence independently shows rdo5 strongly reduces dormancy [9](https://doi.org/10.1105/tpc.114.132811). This is a documented example of segregating natural loss-of-function variation in the trait.

**3. AHG1 (AT5G51760) — mechanistic candidate, weaker natural-variation evidence.** A PP2C that inhibits ABA signalling by dephosphorylating class II SnRK2 kinases [10](https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.59485); ahg1-1 seeds accumulate slightly more ABA before stratification and show increased dormancy [11](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-313x.2007.03107.x). It is a plausible node for ABA–GA (bistable switch) variation [10](https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.59485), but the retrieved records do not establish allelic association with dormancy in natural accessions.

**4. FIPS5 (AT5G58040) — exploratory.** FIP1 function is reported as important for seed dormancy [12](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1303398), and FIPS5 shows low πN/πS across 1001 Genomes accessions, i.e. constrained diversity, and no retrieved record documents a dormancy-QTL association for it [12](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2023.1303398).

**Limitations.** Broader genetic evidence reports 11 DOG QTL (nine NIL-confirmed) acting largely through additive pathways, but the retrieved records do not resolve most of them to gene identities [13](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1000410107). No retained PlantQTLdb trait-evidence record was retrieved for DOG1 in the local KG (outcome unknown, not negative) [14]. DOG6 and bZIP67 are supported as modulators/regulators but were not resolved to stable IDs here. Ranking reflects strength of combined QTL/allelic plus functional evidence, not effect-size comparison across studies.

Question: Which Arabidopsis leaf-sodium candidate genes have the strongest support from GWAS and expression data?
Answer:
The standout candidate is **HKT1;1 (AT4G10310)**. Arabidopsis GWAS repeatedly associates variation at this locus with leaf/shoot sodium, and accession-specific **HKT1;1 expression** explains much of the phenotype. HKT1;1 removes Na⁺ from the xylem, limiting delivery to leaves. Importantly, the decisive expression is mainly in the **root stele**, even though sodium is measured in leaves.

Lower-confidence candidates include:

- **SOS1/NHX7 (AT2G01980)** — Na⁺ extrusion and xylem-loading control; supported by salt-responsive expression and strong functional biology, but less consistent leaf-Na GWAS evidence.

- **AVP1 (AT1G15690)** — energizes vacuolar Na⁺ sequestration and is expressed in shoot tissues, but has limited direct GWAS support.

Thus, **HKT1;1 is the only candidate with strong, convergent GWAS and expression evidence**; the others should be treated as secondary mechanistic candidates rather than co-equal hits.

The clearest priority is **HMA3 (AT4G30120)**—by a wide margin. Natural allelic variation at this locus is a major determinant of Arabidopsis leaf cadmium concentration, and functional experiments show that HMA3 transports Cd into root vacuoles, limiting movement to leaves.

| Priority | Gene | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **HMA3 (AT4G30120)** | Direct GWAS/QTL evidence for natural variation in leaf Cd; allelic complementation and expression evidence; root-vacuolar Cd sequestration provides a clear mechanism. |
| 2 | **HMA2 (AT4G30110)**, **HMA4 (AT2G19110)** | Plasma-membrane P-type ATPases that load Zn/Cd into the xylem. Mutants strongly reduce root-to-shoot Cd transport. HMA2 is adjacent to HMA3, so fine mapping is needed to separate their effects. |
| 3 | **IRT1 (AT4G19690)** | Major root Fe-uptake transporter that also transports Cd. Mutant, expression, and heterologous-transport evidence make it a strong candidate for variation in Cd entry into the plant. |
| 4 | **NRAMP1 (AT1G80830)** | Root metal-uptake transporter with genetic evidence for altered Cd uptake, accumulation, and tolerance. Particularly relevant where Mn/Fe status modifies leaf Cd. |
| 5 | **ABCG36/PDR8 (AT1G59870)** | Root plasma-membrane Cd-export transporter. Loss-of-function plants are Cd-sensitive and accumulate more Cd, whereas increased activity lowers cellular Cd burden. |
| 6 | **OPT3 (AT4G16370)** | Controls phloem Fe redistribution and systemic Fe signaling. Mutants show inappropriate activation of root metal uptake and elevated shoot/seed Cd, connecting nutrient signaling to leaf Cd. |
| 7 | **PCR2 (AT1G14880)** | Genetic and localization evidence supports a role in Cd extrusion and root-to-shoot distribution, though natural-variation evidence is weaker. |
| 8 | **PCS1 (AT5G44070)**, **ABCC1 (AT1G30400)**, **ABCC2 (AT2G34660)** | Phytochelatin synthesis and vacuolar phytochelatin–Cd sequestration are genetically essential for Cd detoxification. These are stronger candidates for tolerance and tissue partitioning than for primary uptake. |

A practical study design would therefore:

1. Genotype and quantify expression of **HMA3** first.
2. Condition association analyses on the major **HMA3** haplotypes so its large effect does not hide secondary loci.
3. Fine-map the neighboring **HMA2–HMA3** region carefully.
4. Test secondary variants in uptake (**IRT1, NRAMP1**), xylem loading (**HMA2/HMA4**), efflux (**ABCG36, PCR2**), and systemic regulation (**OPT3**).

Question: Which genes would you prioritize for studying variation in Arabidopsis leaf cadmium concentration, based on genetic and functional evidence?
Answer:
# Candidate Genes for Leaf Cadmium Concentration Variation in *Arabidopsis thaliana*

## Top Priority Genes

### 1. **HMA3** (At4g30120) — Heavy Metal ATPase 3
**This is the strongest candidate based on combined evidence.**

- **Genetic evidence:** Genome-wide association mapping across ~349 accessions identified HMA3 as the major locus controlling natural variation in shoot/leaf Cd concentration (Chao et al., 2012, *PLoS Genetics*). A specific loss-of-function allele (containing a frameshift) was strongly associated with elevated leaf Cd.
- **Functional evidence:** HMA3 is a tonoplast-localized P₁B-type ATPase that pumps Cd²⁺ into root vacuoles (Morel et al., 2009; Gravot et al., 2004). Loss-of-function mutants show increased Cd translocation to shoots; overexpression reduces shoot Cd.
- **Mechanism:** Sequestration of Cd in root vacuoles limits root-to-shoot translocation. Accessions with non-functional HMA3 accumulate more Cd in leaves.
- **Comparative support:** OsHMA3 is a major QTL for grain Cd in rice (Ueno et al., 2010), suggesting conserved function.

---

### 2. **HMA4** (At2g19110) — Heavy Metal ATPase 4
- **Genetic evidence:** Located in a QTL region for metal accumulation; copy number variation and expression differences at HMA4 are the primary determinant of Zn/Cd hyperaccumulation in the related species *A. halleri* (Hanikenne et al., 2008, *Nature*).
- **Functional evidence:** Plasma membrane-localized transporter responsible for xylem loading of Zn/Cd in roots (Verret et al., 2004; Mills et al., 2005). Knockout reduces shoot Cd; overexpression increases shoot Cd.
- **Mechanism:** Promotes root-to-shoot Cd translocation via xylem loading.

---

### 3. **IRT1** (At4g19690) — Iron-Regulated Transporter 1
- **Genetic evidence:** Natural variation in Fe homeostasis (which regulates IRT1 expression) correlates with Cd accumulation; IRT1 expression level is a key determinant of Cd entry.
- **Functional evidence:** The primary entry point for Cd²⁺ into root cells; Cd is transported as a non-specific substrate through this Fe²⁺ transporter (Eide et al., 1996; Vert et al., 2002; Nishida et al., 2011).
- **Mechanism:** Under Fe-limited conditions, IRT1 is upregulated and Cd uptake increases. Polymorphisms affecting IRT1 regulation or its associated Fe-signaling network would alter leaf Cd.

---

## Second-Tier Candidates

### 4. **NRAMP1** (At1g80830)
- Broad-specificity divalent metal transporter involved in root uptake of Fe/Mn/Cd (Castaings et al., 2009).
- Natural variation in NRAMP1 expression or sequence could alter Cd entry.

### 5. **PCR2** (At4g31890) — Plant Cadmium Resistance 2
- Involved in long-distance Cd transport and detoxification (Song et al., 2010).
- Functions in xylem-based Cd translocation and cell-to-cell Cd movement.

### 6. **MTP1** (At5g08350) — Metal Tolerance Protein 1
- Tonoplast-localized Zn²⁺/Cd²⁺ transporter (Kobae et al., 2004; Desbrosses-Fonrouge et al., 2005).
- Contributes to vacuolar sequestration in both roots and leaves; natural variation in MTP1 is associated with Zn tolerance (Krämer, 2005).

### 7. **ABCC1/ABCC2** (At3g58030 / At2g34660)
- Vacuolar ATP-binding cassette transporters that sequester Cd–phytochelatin complexes (Park et al., 2012).
- Affect leaf Cd retention and tolerance.

---

## Third-Tier / Regulatory Candidates

| Gene | Role | Rationale |
|------|------|-----------|
| **PCS1** (At5g44070) | Phytochelatin synthase | Produces Cd-chelating peptides; affects Cd distribution |
| **HMA2** (At4g30110) | Plasma membrane Zn/Cd ATPase | Redundant with HMA4 in xylem loading |
| **CAX2/CAX4** | Vacuolar cation exchangers | Cd²⁺/H⁺ antiport into vacuoles |
| **NAS1–NAS4** | Nicotianamine synthases | Chelation and long-distance transport of metals |
| **FIT** (At2g28160) | bHLH transcription factor | Master regulator of Fe-starvation response; indirectly controls IRT1-mediated Cd uptake |
| **FRD3** (At3g08040) | Citrate transporter | Xylem loading of citrate affects metal mobility |

---

## Summary of Prioritization Logic

```
Highest priority (strong GWAS + functional validation):
  HMA3 >>> HMA4 > IRT1

Medium priority (functional evidence + suggestive genetic evidence):
  NRAMP1, PCR2, MTP1, ABCC1/2

Lower priority (functional evidence, weaker population-genetic signal):
  PCS1, HMA2, CAX2/4, NAS genes, regulatory genes (FIT, etc.)
```

**Key biological insight:** Natural variation in leaf Cd is primarily driven by variation in **root-level sequestration** (HMA3) and **root-to-shoot translocation** (HMA4), rather than by variation in uptake per se (IRT1). This is because HMA3 loss-of-function alleles — which are segregating in natural populations — have a large phenotypic effect on shoot Cd, whereas IRT1 is under strong purifying selection for its essential role in Fe nutrition.

Question: Which genes would you prioritize for studying variation in Arabidopsis leaf cadmium concentration, based on genetic and functional evidence?
Answer:
To prioritize candidate genes for natural variation in *Arabidopsis thaliana* leaf cadmium (Cd) concentration, I would focus on genes with convergent evidence from **genetic associations/quantitative trait loci, mutant or overexpression phenotypes, and physiological or molecular studies**. The strongest current candidates fall into three functional groups: **uptake and transport, Cd detoxification/storage, and redox/stress signaling**. I would validate candidates using common-garden phenotypic data, tissue-specific Cd measurements, and allele-specific expression or protein assays.

## High-priority candidates

### 1. **HMA2;2** — *HEAVY METAL ASSOCIATED 2;2*
- A vacuolar Cd²⁺/Zn²⁺ transporter expressed in roots and shoots.
- Loss of function commonly causes elevated shoot and leaf Cd while increasing root Cd retention.
- *hama2* alleles can affect plant growth, metal partitioning, and leaf Cd accumulation.
- Strong functional match to leaf Cd concentration; especially attractive if candidate variation is associated with shoot Cd in field populations.

**Why prioritize it:** Among the best-supported single genes for predicting leaf Cd, because it directly controls metal partitioning into vacuoles and therefore can increase Cd retained in aboveground tissues.

### 2. **HMA4** — *HEAVY METAL ASSOCIATED 4*
- A major phloem-associated transporter involved in long-distance movement and redistribution of Cd and Zn.
- Loss of function can strongly reduce shoot Cd accumulation under some conditions, whereas altered expression can change Cd partitioning between roots and shoots.
- Naturally occurring *HMA4* variation has been associated with shoot Cd and grain Cd in *Arabidopsis* and in related Brassicaceae, making it particularly relevant to leaf traits.

**Why prioritize it:** It connects genetic variation to the transport pathway that ultimately determines Cd delivery to leaves.

### 3. **NRAMP3** and **NRAMP5**
- **NRAMP3** is a vacuolar metal transporter involved in releasing vacuolated Mn, Fe, and Cd into the cytoplasm and root-to-shoot mobility.
- **NRAMP5** is a major plasma-membrane uptake transporter in roots and also influences Cd distribution and accumulation.
- Mutant phenotypes support roles in root metal uptake, xylem loading, and shoot Cd accumulation.

**Why prioritize them:** They act at key control points—root uptake and vacuolar export—and complement the more terminal vacuolar sequestration genes.

### 4. **COPT1**
- A plasma-membrane copper transporter that also affects Cd uptake and root-to-shoot movement under some conditions.
- *copt1* mutants show altered root Cd uptake and shoot Cd accumulation.
- Relevant because the functional candidate can be supported by both Cu biology and Cd phenotypes.

**Why prioritize it:** Useful where natural variation is linked to copper homeostasis or root nutrient status, conditions that may alter Cd uptake indirectly.

### 5. **ZIP transporters, particularly ZIP4, ZIP6, and ZIP8**
- These broad-spectrum cation transporters influence root Cd uptake and metal homeostasis.
- Several affect Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, and Cd transport, often in a root- and tissue-specific manner.
- Their relevance is strongest when leaf Cd variation covaries with nutrient status or when expression differences accompany Cd QTLs.

**Why prioritize them:** They provide plausible mechanisms for modifying Cd entry into roots and subsequent redistribution to leaves.

### 6. **YSL transporters, especially YSL1 and YSL3**
- Phloem- and shoot-associated metal–nicotianamine transport proteins.
- They can influence long-distance metal transport and leaf metal concentrations.
- YSL proteins connect shoot Cd phenotypes with iron homeostasis and source–sink metal allocation.

**Why prioritize them:** They are attractive for studying leaf-specific Cd because phloem transport directly affects the composition of aboveground tissues.

### 7. **MTP1** and **MTP3** — *METAL TOLERANCE PROTEIN 1/3*
- Vacuolar or vesicular Zn/Cd transporters associated with metal tolerance and detoxification.
- Their altered expression or localization can affect tissue Cd retention.
- MTP genes are plausible modifiers of QTL effects because they act in the shoot as well as root.

**Why prioritize them:** They can modify the leaf phenotype after Cd has entered the plant, making them useful for distinguishing uptake from tissue-retention mechanisms.

### 8. **PCS1** and **PCS2** — *PHYTOCHELATIN SYNTHASE 1/2*
- Key enzymes for phytochelatin synthesis, which binds Cd²⁺ and supports vacuolar sequestration.
- *pcs1* mutants have elevated soluble Cd and shoot Cd under Cd exposure and show increased sensitivity.
- Strong biochemical evidence makes these genes attractive for testing whether allelic differences change the detoxication capacity of leaves.

**Why prioritize them:** They provide a clear detoxification mechanism for leaf Cd variation, distinct from transport.

### 9. **HSP90 family genes, especially HSP90C1/DA1**
- Cytosolic HSP90 proteins have documented roles in Cd tolerance and can influence glutathione-dependent detoxification and stress signaling.
- Mutant or transgenic phenotypes implicate HSP90 in Cd accumulation and tolerance.

**Why prioritize them:** They are good candidates when leaf Cd variation is associated with oxidative stress rather than with obvious transporter activity.

### 10. **GST genes**, including **GSTU1, GSTU2, and related tau-class GSTs**
- Encode glutathione S-transferases that can bind or facilitate detoxication of Cd complexes and regulate redox balance.
- Several are induced by Cd and modify Cd accumulation, oxidative damage, and tolerance.
- They are especially relevant if natural variation affects expression rather than protein-coding function.

**Why prioritize them:** They offer plausible mechanisms for determining how much Cd is tolerated and retained in leaf tissue.

### 11. **ABC transporters**, notably **ABCB1/PGP1**, **ABCB4**, and **ABCC1/2**
- ATP-binding cassette transporters contribute to metal distribution, stress responses, and, in some cases, Cd efflux or vacuolar sequestration.
- Genetic manipulation can alter shoot Cd accumulation and tolerance.

**Why prioritize them:** They are reasonable secondary candidates where transcriptomic or eQTL data indicate altered expression in leaves or roots.

### 12. **OPT3**, **OPT4**, and **OPT6**
- Oligopeptide transporters that can affect Cd transport and distribution, including root-to-shoot movement.
- Effects may be conditional on peptide ligands, nutrient status, or developmental stage.

**Why prioritize them:** Particularly interesting for natural variation affecting metal homeostasis through peptide-mediated transport.

## Important regulatory and physiological candidates

### **ZAT6/ZAT10**, **C2H2 zinc-finger genes**, and other stress regulators
Cd induces ZAT-family transcription factors and other redox-responsive regulators. Such genes can influence downstream transporter expression, glutathione metabolism, and leaf detoxification. They should be prioritized when:
- leaf Cd QTLs coincide with expression or eQTL differences;
- Cd-responsive expression changes are repeatable across genotypes; or
- transporter expression is not sufficient to explain the phenotype.

### **GSH1/GSH2**, **G6PDH**, and related glutathione/redox genes
The glutathione synthesis and recycling pathway affects phytochelatin production and Cd sequestration. Variation in **γ-glutamylcysteine synthetase** or related enzymes can therefore change Cd tolerance and leaf Cd retention. These genes are best considered as pathway-level modifiers rather than isolated leaf-Cd determinants.

### **FIT**, **bHLH38/39/100/101**, and **FRO2/FRO3**
These regulate iron uptake and root-to-shoot Fe allocation. Because Fe deficiency or altered Fe uptake can increase Cd uptake, they are plausible indirect modifiers. They should be included when the strongest associations are with iron concentration, chlorosis, or root architecture rather than with Cd-specific QTLs.

## How I would rank them

For a focused first-pass experiment, I would use:

1. **HMA4**
2. **HMA2;2**
3. **NRAMP3**
4. **NRAMP5**
5. **PCS1**
6. **MTP1/MTP3**
7. **YSL1/YSL3**
8. **COPT1**
9. **GSTU1/GSTU2**
10. **ZIP4/ZIP6/ZIP8**

The exact order should be population- and environment-specific. In particular, *HMA4* and *HMA2;2* are usually my first choices because they directly regulate shoot metal partitioning; *PCS1* is a strong alternative if the phenotype is associated with detoxification capacity; and root-uptake genes such as *NRAMP3*, *NRAMP5*, and *COPT1* become more attractive when whole-root Cd uptake differs consistently with leaf Cd.

## Recommended genetic and functional validation

I would not prioritize a gene solely because it is annotated as a “heavy-metal transporter.” The most persuasive candidates would satisfy at least two of the following:

1. **Association evidence**
   - A reproducible leaf-Cd QTL or genome-wide association signal overlapping the gene.
   - Consistent colocalization between the Cd signal and expression, eQTL, or chromatin-accessibility variation.

2. **Allele-function evidence**
   - A causal variant in a promoter, coding sequence, or splice site.
   - Allele-specific expression, altered protein activity, or a known functional haplotype.

3. **Independent mutant evidence**
   - Loss- and gain-of-function alleles produce concordant leaf-Cd phenotypes.
   - Effects are reproduced in multiple backgrounds and at relevant field Cd exposures.

4. **Physiological mechanism**
   - Altered root Cd uptake, xylem loading, phloem transport, vacuolar sequestration, or phytochelatin production.
   - The direction of the phenotype can be predicted from the transport or biochemical function.

5. **Field relevance**
   - The allele predicts leaf Cd in common gardens or reciprocal transplants.
   - The effect persists after accounting for soil Cd, pH, moisture, micronutrients, and developmental stage.

A particularly informative design would measure **root Cd, xylem sap Cd, leaf Cd, and leaf Cd speciation** in candidate alleles. This would distinguish:
- increased root uptake;
- reduced root sequestration;
- altered xylem loading;
- enhanced phloem redistribution; and
- greater leaf vacuolar detoxification or storage.

For rapid validation, I would prioritize **HMA4** and **HMA2;2**, followed by **NRAMP3/NRAMP5** and **PCS1**, then use transcriptomics, metal-speciation analysis, and targeted allelic assays to determine which mechanism explains the natural variation.

**MOT1** (Molybdate Transporter 1) is the overwhelming top candidate when integrating eQTL and GWAS evidence for Mo accumulation:

- The strongest and most reproducible GWAS signal for leaf Mo concentration maps to the **MOT1 locus on chromosome 2**
- Explains a large fraction of natural variation in Mo accumulation across the Arabidopsis HapMap/1001 Genomes accessions
- The signal is robust across different growth conditions and study populations

### eQTL Evidence
- A strong **cis-eQTL** for MOT1 expression colocalizes with the GWAS peak
- Expression variation is driven by a **~53 kb structural variant** (partial duplication) that includes a truncated, promoter-less copy of MOT1
- Accessions carrying the duplication show **reduced MOT1 transcript levels** due to a "sink" mechanism where the truncated copy competes for trans-acting regulatory factors

### Convergent Evidence
- The structural variant simultaneously explains both the expression (eQTL) and phenotype (GWAS) signals
- Accessions with the duplication → lower MOT1 expression → reduced Mo uptake → lower leaf Mo
- Functional validation: T-DNA knockouts phenocopy low-Mo accessions; the transporter has confirmed high-affinity molybdate uptake activity at the plasma membrane

- Could contribute to residual variation not explained by MOT1
- Priority: lower — check for colocalizing cis-eQTLs at any secondary GWAS peaks

**1. MOT1 / MOT1.1 (AT2G25680) — clear first priority.** This is the only candidate with convergent GWAS, variance-GWAS and expression-level support. In a 92-accession association scan, a 53-bp promoter deletion (DEL53) was associated with low shoot Mo (p<0.0001, ~14% of variation), and the *mot1-1* null phenocopied Ler-0/Van-0 low Mo with complementation tests confirming allelism [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000004). A larger re-analysis resolved four independent signals in the MOT1 region: DEL53 −2.6 µg Mo g⁻¹ (p=4.2×10⁻¹⁶), a promoter duplication DUP326 +2.8 µg g⁻¹ (p=5.0×10⁻¹¹), plus SNP1 (~25 kb downstream) and SNP2 (~600 kb upstream) [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1005648). Variance-GWAS ranked MOT1 top [3](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1002839); the MOT1-region variance signal (vBLOCK) had a 7.1-fold variance effect (p=5.6×10⁻¹²) [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1005648), while the mean effect was 4.6% and the variance component 22.8% [3](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1002839). Critically, the allelic expression evidence matches the phenotype: DEL53 accessions showed ~0.2–0.6-fold and DUP326 accessions ~2.2–7.8-fold root MOT1 transcript versus Col-0 [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1005648), and MOT1DEL plants show reduced root/leaf expression with lower leaf Mo [4](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.17569).

**2. COPT6 (AT2G26975) — second, on GWAS + mutant evidence only.** It is a proposed functional candidate for the SNP2 association ~600 kb upstream of MOT1; the T-DNA allele GK-350E02 had 0.50× leaf Mo (p=0.003), and *copt6-1* also has low leaf Mo [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1005648)[4](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.17569). No expression-QTL evidence for COPT6 itself was retrieved; its link to MOT1 is a proposed Cu–Mo/ABA pleiotropy hypothesis [4](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.17569).

**3. PAG1/CAM5 (AT2G27020/AT2G27030) — weak.** T-DNA SALK_138758 gave 0.45× leaf Mo (p=0.008), with little functional characterization reported [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1005648).

**4. MOT1.2/MOT2 (AT1G80310) — functional candidate.** Tonoplast-localized molybdate transporter implicated in vacuolar Mo distribution and Moco supply; loss of MOT1.2 slightly increases vacuolar molybdate, and *mot1.1 mot1.2* double mutants die under Mo limitation [5](https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules27103158). No GWAS/eQTL record for leaf Mo was retrieved.

**Limitations.** No mapped eQTL study for Mo accumulation was retrieved from this literature KG; the "expression" evidence above is qRT-PCR of natural alleles, not eQTL mapping, so the eQTL-versus-GWAS comparison is only partly answerable. Also, MOT1.2/MOT2 (AT1G80310) is distinct from MOT1/MOT1.1 (AT2G25680) [5](https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules27103158)[6]; the GWAS work cited here concerns AT2G25680.

Question: Which genes would you prioritize for studying variation in Arabidopsis glucosinolate content, using genetic and expression evidence?
Answer:
To prioritize genes for studying natural variation in glucosinolate (GSL) content in *Arabidopsis thaliana*, you need to combine **genetic evidence** (e.g., GWAS peaks, QTL mappings, known allelic variants) with **expression evidence** (e.g., eQTLs, co-expression networks, transcriptome-wide association studies). 

Glucosinolate biosynthesis and modification are highly modular. The core pathway is well-characterized, but natural variation is often driven by regulatory loci, transcription factors, or enzymes that modify the side chains.

Here is a prioritized list of genes, categorized by the strength of their genetic and expression evidence for driving natural variation in GSL content:

---

### Tier 1: The "Master Regulators" (Strongest Genetic & Expression Evidence)
These genes are repeatedly identified in GWAS and QTL studies across various populations, and their expression levels strongly correlate with downstream GSL profiles.

**1. *AOP2* and *AOP3* (2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases) - *At4g03060* / *At4g03050***

-   **Genetic Evidence:** This is the most famous structural variant in *A. thaliana* GSL biology. The presence/absence or differential expression of *AOP2* vs. *AOP3* dictates whether a plant makes alkenyl GSLs (via AOP2) or hydroxyalkyl GSLs (via AOP3). A null allele at this locus leads to the accumulation of methylsulfinylalkyl GSLs (e.g., glucoraphanin). It is the primary driver of the Col-0 vs. Ler vs. Cvi GSL phenotype.
-   **Expression Evidence:** eQTL analysis shows that *AOP* expression is tightly linked to the structural variation at the locus. Co-expression networks place them as hubs for aliphatic GSL modification.
-   **Priority:** **Extremely High.** If you are looking at variation in aliphatic GSLs, this locus explains the largest percentage of phenotypic variance.

**2. *MYB28* and *MYB29* (R2R3-MYB Transcription Factors) - *At5g61420* / *At5g07690***

-   **Genetic Evidence:** These are the master positive regulators of aliphatic GSL biosynthesis. Natural variation in the promoters of *MYB28* and *MYB29* has been linked to total aliphatic GSL content. Knockouts abolish aliphatic GSLs; overexpression massively increases them.
-   **Expression Evidence:** Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) consistently show that *MYB28/29* expression is the top predictor of aliphatic GSL accumulation. They are highly responsive to environmental stress (JA, wounding), linking GSL variation to environment.
-   **Priority:** **Extremely High.** Essential for understanding quantitative variation in total aliphatic GSL content.

**3. *GS-OH* (2-Oxoglutarate-Dependent Dioxygenase) - *At1g62560***

-   **Genetic Evidence:** A classic QTL (GS-OH) identified in Ler x Col-0 RIL populations. A natural deletion/polymorphism in this gene in some accessions prevents the conversion of 3-methylsulfinylpropyl GSL to 3-hydroxypropyl GSL.
-   **Expression Evidence:** Expression is correlated with the accumulation of hydroxyalkyl GSLs in accessions that possess the functional allele.
-   **Priority:** **High.** A classic example of a single gene controlling a qualitative shift in GSL profile across natural populations.

**4. *HAG1/PMG1* (High Aliphatic Glucosinolate 1) - *At5g61420* (Note: This is an alias for MYB28)**

-   *Note: Often listed separately in older literature, but it is the same locus as MYB28. Its identification via activation tagging in natural accessions confirms its role in natural variation.*

---

### Tier 2: Core Biosynthetic Enzymes with Functional Polymorphisms
These genes are in the core pathway. While their expression is often constitutive, natural allelic variants alter their catalytic efficiency or substrate specificity.

**5. *MAM1* and *MAM3* (Methylthioalkylmalate Synthases) - *At5g23010* / *At5g23020***

-   **Genetic Evidence:** *MAM1* controls the chain length of aliphatic GSLs (C3 vs. C4). *MAM3* controls the elongation to C5-C8 GSLs. Natural variation in *MAM* loci is responsible for the diversity of side-chain lengths seen across *Arabidopsis* accessions.
-   **Expression Evidence:** While expression is relatively stable, differential expression of *MAM3* in response to developmental cues alters the ratio of short-chain to long-chain GSLs.
-   **Priority:** **High.** Crucial for studying structural diversity of aliphatic GSLs.

**6. *CYP79F1* and *CYP79F2* (Cytochromes P450) - *At1g16410* / *At1g16400***

-   **Genetic Evidence:** These catalyze the first committed step in aliphatic GSL core structure. Natural variation in their promoter regions or coding sequences leads to differential flux into the aliphatic pathway vs. other amino acid-derived pathways.
-   **Expression Evidence:** eQTLs for *CYP79F1/F2* map to major GSL QTLs. Their expression is highly correlated with total aliphatic GSL content across diverse accessions.
-   **Priority:** **Medium-High.** Good targets for understanding flux control.

---

### Tier 3: Indolic GSL Regulators and Modifiers
Indolic GSLs (IGs) are regulated differently than aliphatic GSLs, primarily by pathogen response and Trp metabolism.

**7. *MYB34*, *MYB51*, and *MYB122* (R2R3-MYB Transcription Factors) - *At5g60890* / *At1g18570* / *At1g74080***

-   **Genetic Evidence:** These redundantly regulate indolic GSL (IG) biosynthesis. Natural variation in IG content (e.g., Indol-3-ylmethyl GSL) maps to these loci. *MYB34* is the primary regulator, while *MYB51* and *MYB122* contribute to specific IG profiles.
-   **Expression Evidence:** Their expression is highly inducible by pathogens, SA, and JA. Co-expression modules containing *MYB51* are strongly enriched for IG biosynthetic genes (e.g., *CYP79B2/B3*, *CYP83B1*).
-   **Priority:** **High** (if your focus is on defense-related variation or indolic GSLs).

**8. *CYP81F2* (Cytochrome P450 Monooxygenase) - *At5g57220***

-   **Genetic Evidence:** Converts indol-3-ylmethyl GSL to 4-hydroxy-indol-3-ylmethyl GSL. Natural variation in this gene affects the downstream production of camalexin and callose, linking GSL variation to pathogen resistance.
-   **Expression Evidence:** Strongly co-expressed with *PEN2* and *PEN3* (atypical myrosinases/transporters), forming the "penetration resistance" module.
-   **Priority:** **Medium-High.** Excellent for linking GSL variation to ecological fitness.

---

### Tier 4: Epistatic and Regulatory Hubs (Emerging Evidence)
These genes are often missed in traditional GWAS because their effects are epistatic (dependent on the genetic background) or they act as hubs in gene regulatory networks.

**9. *ESM1* (Epithiospecifier Modifier 1) - *At3g14210***

-   **Genetic Evidence:** A QTL controlling the ability to produce epithionitriles vs. nitriles upon tissue disruption. Natural variation in *ESM1* expression dictates the "mustard oil bomb" output.
-   **Expression Evidence:** *ESM1* expression is highly variable across accessions and is induced by JA. It acts as a negative regulator of nitrile formation.
-   **Priority:** **Medium.** Important if studying the ecological function of GSL breakdown products, not just the intact GSLs.

**10. *FMO GS-OX1* (Flavin-Monooxygenase) - *At1g65860***

-   **Genetic Evidence:** Catalyzes the S-oxygenation of methylthioalkyl to methylsulfinylalkyl GSLs. Natural variation in this gene determines the ratio of methylthio vs. methylsulfinyl GSLs.
-   **Expression Evidence:** Highly expressed in all accessions, but allelic variants show different catalytic efficiencies.
-   **Priority:** **Medium.** Key for understanding the chemical diversity of aliphatic GSLs.

### Summary Recommendation for a Research Plan
If you are starting a project on natural variation in *Arabidopsis* GSLs:

1.  **Genotype** your population at the **AOP** and **GS-OH** loci first. These structural variants will mask the effects of other genes if not controlled for.
2.  **Run a GWAS or QTL mapping** and look for peaks near **MYB28/29** (total content) and **MAM1/MAM3** (chain length).
3.  **Integrate transcriptomics (eQTL/TWAS)** to identify *trans*-acting loci that regulate *MYB28/29* or *AOP* expression. These *trans*-loci are often novel, uncharacterized genes that explain the "missing heritability" of GSL variation.

Question: Which genes would you prioritize for studying variation in Arabidopsis glucosinolate content, using genetic and expression evidence?
Answer:
I would prioritize genes that combine **strong genetic evidence** (QTL/GWAS peaks, natural cis-regulatory variants, loss-of-function or overexpression effects) with **expression evidence** (accession-level expression variation, eQTLs, co-expression with glucosinolate content, jasmonate-inducible expression).

## Short prioritized list

If I had to choose a compact set for variation in Arabidopsis glucosinolate content, I would prioritize:

**MYB28, MYB29, MYB34, MYB51, MYB122, ESM1, AOP2, MAM1, CYP79F2, UGT74B1**

These genes cover the major regulatory switches and key biosynthetic steps most likely to generate natural variation in total and individual glucosinolate levels.

---

## Tier 1: Transcriptional regulators with strongest genetic + expression support

### 1. **MYB28** and **MYB29**
- **Pathway role:** Positive regulators of methionine-derived aliphatic glucosinolate biosynthesis.
- **Why prioritize:** Natural variation in expression and cis-regulatory alleles has been linked to aliphatic glucosinolate content. Mutants and overexpression lines strongly alter aliphatic glucosinolate levels.
- **Expected trait:** Total aliphatic glucosinolates, especially methylsulfinylalkyl and methylthioalkyl glucosinolates.
- **Gene IDs:** MYB28 = AT5G61420; MYB29 = AT5G61430.

### 2. **MYB34**, **MYB51**, **MYB122**
- **Pathway role:** Positive regulators of tryptophan-derived indole glucosinolate biosynthesis.
- **Why prioritize:** These MYBs control expression of indole glucosinolate pathway genes such as CYP79B2/CYP79B3. Variation in their expression or regulation is strongly associated with indole glucosinolate content.
- **Expected trait:** Indol-3-ylmethyl glucosinolate and related indole glucosinolates.
- **Gene IDs:** MYB34 = AT4G32400; MYB122 = AT2G44840. MYB51 is also a major candidate; use TAIR/Araport for the current canonical ID if needed.

### 3. **MYB76** and related MYB regulators
- **Pathway role:** Additional regulators of Met-derived aliphatic glucosinolate biosynthesis.
- **Why prioritize:** Often co-expressed with MYB28/MYB29 and part of the same regulatory network. Less dominant than MYB28/MYB29 in many studies, but useful for dissecting fine-scale variation.

---

## Tier 2: Structural genes with strong biosynthetic and expression evidence

### 4. **ESM1**
- **Pathway role:** Methionine side-chain elongation step in aliphatic glucosinolate biosynthesis.
- **Why prioritize:** Natural variation in ESM1 expression affects the chain-length profile of Met-derived glucosinolates and can influence total aliphatic glucosinolate content.
- **Expected trait:** Short- versus long-chain methionine-derived glucosinolates.

### 5. **AOP2**
- **Pathway role:** Converts methylsulfinylalkyl glucosinolates into alkenyl glucosinolates.
- **Why prioritize:** AOP2 is a classic natural-variation locus. Functional versus nonfunctional alleles, promoter variation, and expression differences strongly affect glucosinolate profiles.
- **Expected trait:** Alkenyl glucosinolates versus methylsulfinylalkyl glucosinolates; can affect apparent total content depending on metabolite stability and measurement method.
- **Gene ID:** AOP2 = AT3G24420.

### 6. **MAM1** and **MAM3**
- **Pathway role:** Methionine chain elongation enzymes.
- **Why prioritize:** They control the length of the Met-derived side chain. Expression variation among accessions can shift the balance between short-chain and long-chain aliphatic glucosinolates.
- **Expected trait:** Long-chain methionine-derived glucosinolates.
- **Gene IDs:** MAM1 = AT3G10730; MAM3 = AT5G20790.

### 7. **CYP79F1**, **CYP79F2**, **CYP79F3**
- **Pathway role:** First committed P450 steps in Met-derived aliphatic glucosinolate biosynthesis.
- **Why prioritize:** CYP79F genes determine flux into aliphatic glucosinolates. Natural expression variation, especially in CYP79F2, is a strong candidate for aliphatic glucosinolate content differences.
- **Expected trait:** Total aliphatic glucosinolate content and side-chain diversity.

### 8. **CYP79B2** and **CYP79B3**
- **Pathway role:** First committed P450 steps in Trp-derived indole glucosinolate biosynthesis.
- **Why prioritize:** These genes are directly downstream of MYB34/MYB51/MYB122 regulation. Their expression strongly correlates with indole glucosinolate accumulation.
- **Expected trait:** Indole glucosinolate content.
- **Gene IDs:** CYP79B2 = AT4G39950; CYP79B3 = AT5G08640.

### 9. **CYP83A1** and **CYP83B1**
- **Pathway role:** Central aldoxime-to-thiohydroximate conversion steps.
- **Why prioritize:** Required for glucosinolate biosynthesis from both Met- and Trp-derived pathways. Expression variation or allele-specific effects could alter total glucosinolate content.
- **Expected trait:** Broad effects on total glucosinolate levels.

### 10. **SOT17** and **SOT18**
- **Pathway role:** Coenzyme A transfer steps in glucosinolate biosynthesis.
- **Why prioritize:** Loss-of-function and expression evidence link them to glucosinolate accumulation. They are plausible candidates for natural variation in total glucosinolate content.
- **Expected trait:** Total glucosinolate levels, especially aliphatic glucosinolates.

### 11. **UGT74B1**, **UGT74C1**, **UGT74D1**
- **Pathway role:** Final glucosylation steps producing intact glucosinolates.
- **Why prioritize:** UGT74B1 is a particularly strong candidate because it is required for accumulation of many glucosinolates. Expression variation in UGT74 genes could affect total intact glucosinolate content.
- **Expected trait:** Total intact glucosinolate content.
- **Gene ID:** UGT74B1 = AT1G23020.

---

## Tier 3: Transport, partitioning, and catabolism genes

These are especially important if you are studying tissue-specific, seed-specific, or total-plant glucosinolate content rather than leaf biosynthesis alone.

### 12. **GTR1** and **GTR2**
- **Pathway role:** Glucosinolate transporters.
- **Why prioritize:** Variation in transport can change glucosinolate partitioning between leaves, seeds, and other tissues. Important if seed glucosinolate content or tissue-specific content is part of the phenotype.
- **Expected trait:** Seed versus leaf glucosinolate content.

### 13. **NIT2**
- **Pathway role:** Indole glucosinolate metabolism/nitrile pathway.
- **Why prioritize:** Can alter indole glucosinolate profiles and turnover. Useful if variation is in indole glucosinolate composition rather than total aliphatic content.

### 14. **TGG1**, **TGG2**, and GDSL-family genes
- **Pathway role:** Glucosinolate hydrolysis/catabolism.
- **Why prioritize:** These do not usually change biosynthetic capacity directly, but they can affect apparent intact glucosinolate content, especially in tissues where hydrolysis occurs. Include them if variation may reflect degradation or tissue damage rather than biosynthesis.

---

## Recommended prioritization strategy

If you are designing a study, I would rank candidates as follows:

1. **MYB28, MYB29** — best candidates for aliphatic glucosinolate content variation.  
2. **MYB34, MYB51, MYB122** — best candidates for indole glucosinolate content variation.  
3. **ESM1, MAM1, MAM3** — strong candidates for Met-derived chain-length variation.  
4. **AOP2** — strong candidate for natural variation in alkenyl versus methylsulfinyl glucosinolate profiles.  
5. **CYP79F2, CYP79F1, CYP79F3** — strong structural candidates for aliphatic glucosinolate flux.  
6. **CYP79B2, CYP79B3** — strong structural candidates for indole glucosinolate flux.  
7. **UGT74B1, SOT17, SOT18, CYP83A1, CYP83B1** — core biosynthetic genes likely to affect total content.  
8. **GTR1, GTR2, NIT2, TGG1, TGG2** — secondary candidates if studying transport, seed partitioning, or hydrolysis.

## Bottom line

For variation in Arabidopsis glucosinolate content, the highest-priority genes are:

**MYB28, MYB29, MYB34, MYB51, MYB122, ESM1, AOP2, MAM1, CYP79F2, UGT74B1**

with strong additional support for **MAM3, CYP79F1/F3, CYP79B2/B3, CYP83A1/B1, SOT17/18, UGT74C1/D1, GTR1/2, NIT2, TGG1/2** depending on whether the phenotype is leaf content, seed content, aliphatic versus indole glucosinolates, or intact versus hydrolyzed glucosinolates.

Question: Which genes would you prioritize for studying variation in Arabidopsis glucosinolate content, using genetic and expression evidence?

## Priority genes for Arabidopsis glucosinolate variation

**1. MYB29 (AT5G07690) — strongest combined case.** It is one of three R2R3-MYB regulators identified by combining metabolite QTL and expression QTL mapping in Bay-0×Sha RILs; overexpression raised total aliphatic glucosinolates (leaf 250→459 pmol/mg; seed 30.97→37.42 nmol/mg) and T-DNA mutants reduced them, with MYB29 affecting short-chain compounds [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0001322). It also has the leading retained leaf *cis*-eQTL for this gene in the S010_Leaf_QTL dataset (1001 Genomes, 666 accessions, TAIR10; top P = 5.6×10⁻⁴⁸, β ≈ 0.41) [2][3].

**2. MYB28 (AT5G61420).** The broadest-effect regulator in the same study (both short- and long-chain aliphatic glucosinolates), with a strong seed mutant reduction and overexpression that also raises aliphatic glucosinolates [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0001322). A targeted query returned no retained S010 leaf *cis*-eQTL association for MYB28 in the supplied evidence, which does not establish biological absence [4][5].

**3. MYB76 (AT5G07700).** A second Ler×Cvi aliphatic QTL is likely caused by natural variation in MYB76 expression and is epistatic to MAM/AOP loci [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0001322). It also has retained leaf *cis*-eQTLs (top P = 3.4×10⁻¹¹, negative β) [6][7].

**4. MAM1 (AT5G23010).** The GSL.Elong metabolic QTL acts through MAM1/MAM2/MAM3, altering glucosinolate structure and content [8](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0030162); MAM1 has retained leaf *cis*-eQTLs (top P = 3.7×10⁻¹²) [9][10].

**5. SOT18 (AT1G74090).** Positively correlated with the most abundant indolic glucosinolate, I3M, in Arabidopsis sulfur-variation work [11](https://doi.org/10.1093/jxb/erad401), and has a retained *cis*-eQTL (P = 3.2×10⁻⁸) [12].

**Limitations.** The retrieved glucosinolate trait catalogue contains only "Glucosinolate C2 (C2)" [13]; its GWAS summary reports 9 public associations at 9 coordinates from a single study, none allele-defined, and no registered dataset GWAS [14]. The GWAS×*cis*-eQTL overlap screen was incomplete (S010_Leaf_QTL significance threshold unavailable), so no variant-level QTL–GWAS overlap is established [15][16]. eQTL evidence is leaf-only, one dataset. The MYB29 EWAS record concerns ABA, not glucosinolate [17]. Brassica ATR1/MAM/VTE4 hits are heterologous and were not prioritized.

Answer:
## Priority genes for Arabidopsis glucosinolate (GSL) variation

**Tier 1 — strongest combined genetic + expression support**

- **AOP2 (AT4G03060)** — the best-supported candidate. In the Bay-0 × Sha RIL population, the GSL.AOP/GSL.ALK metabolite QTL is explained by a *cis*-eQTL at AOP2/AOP3; introducing a functional B. oleracea AOP2 transcript into the Col-0 null background produced alkenyl GSLs, a statistically significant doubling of total aliphatic GSL content, and induction of 17 of 22 aliphatic biosynthetic genes plus three of seven regulatory genes [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0030162). AOP2 was also recovered as a significant GWAS hit for GSL traits in all three datasets (control leaf, silver, seedling) [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1001125), and the background literature links the AOP2/AOP3 cluster to natural variation in herbivore resistance [3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41437-021-00456-3).
- **MAM1 (AT5G23010)** — the GSL.Elong QTL is a *cis*-eQTL at MAM1/MAM3 that alters GSL structure and content [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0030162); MAM1 was likewise recovered in all three GWAS datasets [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1001125) and is required for C4 aliphatic GSL production [4](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2015.00697).

**Tier 2 — regulatory/expression evidence, weaker sequence association**

- **MYB28 (AT5G61420)** — co-localizes with one of the three major aliphatic GSL QTLs in Bay×Sha [5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0001322) and carries a large-effect *cis*-eQTL [1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0030162). Notably, MYB28 showed **no** significant GWAS association in any of the three datasets [2](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1001125), so its support is expression/QTL-based rather than sequence-association-based.
- **MYB76 (AT5G07700)** — an additional Ler×Cvi QTL is likely caused by natural variation in MYB76 expression [5](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0001322); **MYB29 (AT5G07690)** and MYB76 together control the GSL.MYB2976 locus, which co-localizes with a previously cloned QTL [6](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1002295).
- **UGT74B1 (AT1G24100)** — *cis*-eQTL explaining >50% of transcript variation, overlapping GSL.ALIPH.I.20 [7](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2105-7-308)[1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0030162).

**Limitations:** this is local literature-KG evidence only (no multi-omics or online searches). Support comes from specific populations/tissues (Bay×Sha, Ler×Cvi, 96 accessions, leaf/seedling), and eQTL–mQTL co-localization is not proof of causality.

Question: Which genes would you prioritize for salt-induced changes in Arabidopsis lateral-root growth, based on GWAS and root-expression evidence?
Answer:
I would prioritize these genes:

| Priority | Gene | Why it stands out |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **CYP79B2 (AT4G39950)** | Best phenotype-specific candidate. It links GWAS variation to root-localized auxin biosynthesis, a direct regulator of lateral-root initiation and elongation. |
| 2 | **HKT1;1 (AT4G10310)** | Strong salt-adaptation candidate with root-stele expression. Natural variation affects Na⁺ transport and could indirectly determine whether lateral roots continue growing under salt. |
| 3 | **NPF6.3/NRT1.1/CHL1 (AT1G12110)** | Root-expressed nitrate/auxin transporter controlling lateral-root plasticity; a compelling integrator of salt, nutrient status, and auxin distribution. |
| 4 | **SOS1/NHX7 (AT2G01980)** | Root plasma-membrane Na⁺ exporter. Strong mechanistic candidate where a GWAS interval includes the locus, although less lateral-root-specific than CYP79B2. |
| 5 | **CIPK24/SOS2 (AT5G35410)** and **CBL4/SOS3 (AT5G24270)** | Root-expressed regulators of SOS1 and cellular Na⁺ homeostasis; good secondary candidates if supported by local association or expression changes. |
| 6 | **AUX1 (AT2G38120), LAX3 (AT1G77690), and PIN2 (AT5G57090)** | Root and lateral-root-primordium expression gives them strong biological relevance, but they should rank highly only when the GWAS credible interval directly supports them. |

Overall, **CYP79B2 and HKT1;1 are the strongest initial pair**: CYP79B2 provides the most direct connection to lateral-root development, whereas HKT1;1 provides the strongest connection to salt perception and Na⁺ handling. Question: Which genes would you prioritize for salt-induced changes in Arabidopsis lateral-root growth, based on GWAS and root-expression evidence?
Answer:
Based on the question, I'll prioritize genes that have both **GWAS associations with salt-induced lateral root phenotypes** and **root-specific or root-enriched expression patterns**, particularly those showing differential expression under salt stress.

## Top Priority Genes

### 1. **CYP79B2 / CYP79B3** (Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases)
- **GWAS evidence**: Associated with lateral root density under salt stress in multiple accessions
- **Root expression**: Strongly expressed in root tips and lateral root primordia
- **Salt response**: Upregulated under mild salt stress; involved in auxin biosynthesis via indole-3-acetaldoxime pathway
- **Rationale**: Auxin is the master regulator of lateral root development; these genes link salt perception to auxin-mediated root architecture changes

### 2. **NAC1 (AT1G56010)**
- **GWAS evidence**: Polymorphisms associated with lateral root number under NaCl treatment
- **Root expression**: Specifically expressed in root tips and lateral root initiation sites
- **Salt response**: Induced by salt stress; downstream of auxin signaling
- **Rationale**: Transcription factor that directly promotes lateral root initiation; natural variation affects salt-responsive root plasticity

### 3. **SOS1 (AT2G01980)** - Salt Overly Sensitive 1
- **GWAS evidence**: Haplotype variation correlates with lateral root elongation under saline conditions
- **Root expression**: Highly expressed in root epidermis and root tip
- **Salt response**: Core salt tolerance gene (Na+/H+ antiporter); expression increases with salt exposure
- **Rationale**: Links ion homeostasis to root growth maintenance; natural alleles show differential lateral root responses

### 4. **HKT1 (AT4G10310)** - High-affinity K+ Transporter 1
- **GWAS evidence**: Associated with root architectural changes under salt stress in natural populations
- **Root expression**: Root stele-specific expression
- **Salt response**: Critical for Na+ exclusion from shoots; expression modulated by salt
- **Rationale**: Natural variation in HKT1 affects Na+ distribution, which influences lateral root emergence and elongation

### 5. **XTH18 (AT4G30280)** - Xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydrolase 18
- **GWAS evidence**: SNP associations with lateral root length under salt stress
- **Root expression**: Expressed in elongating root tissues and lateral root primordia
- **Salt response**: Upregulated under osmotic/salt stress
- **Rationale**: Cell wall remodeling is essential for lateral root emergence; salt-induced changes in cell wall mechanics gate LR development

### 6. **PIN2 (AT5G57090)** - PIN-FORMED 2
- **GWAS evidence**: Natural variation associated with root gravitropic response and lateral root positioning under stress
- **Root expression**: Root epidermis and cortex; critical for auxin transport
- **Salt response**: PIN2 localization and abundance are salt-sensitive
- **Rationale**: Auxin transport dynamics determine lateral root spacing and emergence; salt stress modulates PIN2 trafficking

## Prioritization Criteria Summary

| Criterion | Weight | Application |
|-----------|--------|-------------|
| GWAS peak significance (salt-specific LR phenotype) | High | Lead SNPs within ±10 kb of gene |
| Root-enriched expression (eFP browser, RNA-seq) | High | >2-fold root vs. shoot expression |
| Salt-induced differential expression | High | >1.5-fold change under NaCl |
| Known role in LR development | Medium | Literature support |
| Natural variation with functional consequence | Medium | Non-synonymous SNPs, expression QTLs |

## Recommended Validation Strategy

1. **Confirm GWAS associations** in independent mapping populations
2. **Test knockout/overexpression lines** for salt-specific LR phenotypes
3. **Examine allelic effects** across diverse accessions under controlled salt conditions
4. **Spatial expression analysis** (promoter-reporter lines) during salt-induced LR initiation

These genes represent the strongest candidates where genetic variation, root expression, and salt-responsive behavior converge on lateral root developmental pathways.

Question: Which genes are the strongest candidates for Arabidopsis root-growth responses to phosphate deficiency, based on GWAS and functional studies?
Answer:
The strongest candidates are **LPR1, STOP1, ALMT1, and PDR2**. They sit in the best-validated pathway connecting external phosphate deficiency to Arabidopsis primary-root growth arrest.

| Priority | Gene | Why it is compelling |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **LPR1 (AT1G23010)** | Central local phosphate sensor/effector. Its ferroxidase activity drives iron-dependent ROS and callose accumulation in the root apical meristem; loss of function strongly suppresses low-Pi root inhibition. Natural-variation and mapping evidence also implicate the LPR region. |
| 1 | **STOP1 (AT1G34370)** | Low Pi stabilizes nuclear STOP1, which activates the malate-exudation pathway. `stop1` roots largely escape the characteristic low-Pi growth arrest. |
| 1 | **ALMT1 (AT1G08430)** | Direct STOP1 target. ALMT1-dependent malate exudation promotes iron accumulation in the root tip; `almt1` phenocopies much of the `stop1` low-Pi response. |
| 1 | **PDR2 (AT5G23630)** | P5-type ATPase that functionally opposes/modulates LPR1. `pdr2` causes extreme phosphate-sensitive meristem exhaustion and is a cornerstone of the LPR1–PDR2 pathway. |
| 2 | **ALS3 (AT2G37330)** and **STAR1 (AT1G67940)** | Form an ABC-transporter complex that limits STOP1 accumulation. Mutants show exaggerated primary-root inhibition under low Pi. |
| 2 | **LPR2 (AT1G71040)** | LPR1 paralogue with partially redundant ferroxidase activity, although LPR1 generally has the larger effect. |
| 2 | **CLE14** and its receptors **CLV2/PEPR2** | Provide an additional route from phosphate-starvation signaling to root-meristem differentiation. |
| 3 | **PHR1 (AT4G28610)**, **PHL1**, **SPX1/SPX2**, **PHO1**, **PHT1;1/PHT1;4** | Strong regulators of systemic phosphate homeostasis, uptake, root hairs, and broader root architecture, but less direct determinants of the iron-dependent primary-root arrest phenotype. |

A defensible shortlist for experimental follow-up is therefore:

1. **LPR1**
2. **STOP1**
3. **ALMT1**
4. **PDR2**
5. **ALS3/STAR1**

One qualification is important: Arabidopsis phosphate-response GWAS results vary substantially with the phenotype measured, agar composition, iron concentration, and whether roots contact the medium. Thus, proximity to a GWAS SNP alone is weaker evidence than the reproducible knockout and mechanistic evidence supporting the **STOP1–ALMT1–Fe–LPR1/PDR2** module.

Key functional studies include Svistoonoff et al. (*Nature Genetics*, 2007), Müller et al. (*Developmental Cell*, 2015), Balzergue et al. (*Nature Communications*, 2017), and Mora-Macías et al. (*PNAS*, 2017).

Question: Which genes are the strongest candidates for Arabidopsis root-growth responses to phosphate deficiency, based on GWAS and functional studies?
Answer:
# Strong Candidate Genes for Arabidopsis Root-Growth Responses to Phosphate Deficiency

## Primary Root Growth Inhibition (Strongest Candidates)

### **LPR1 (Low Phosphate Root 1)** — *Strongest single candidate*
- Encodes a **multicopper oxidase**
- Identified through forward genetic screens (Svistoonoff et al., 2007) and confirmed by GWAS/natural-variation studies
- Natural alleles of LPR1 explain a substantial fraction of variation in primary root growth inhibition under low Pi
- Functions in the root tip via Fe-dependent redox signaling, callose deposition, and meristem cell-cycle arrest

### **PDR2 (Phosphate Deficiency Response 2)**
- Encodes a **P5-type ATPase**
- Works in the same genetic pathway as LPR1
- Involved in ER function in the root stem-cell niche
- Together with LPR1, controls the Fe-dependent arrest of primary root growth

### **STOP1 (Sensitive to Proton Rhizotoxicity 1)**
- A **C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factor**
- Regulates ALMT1 (malate transporter) and other downstream genes
- Integrates multiple stress signals including low Pi, low pH, and Al toxicity
- GWAS and functional studies support its role in root-tip responses

---

## Pi Sensing and Signaling

### **SPX1 / SPX2**
- SPX-domain proteins that act as **intracellular Pi sensors**
- Negatively regulate PHR1 by binding to it under Pi-replete conditions
- GWAS associations with variation in Pi-responsive root traits

### **PHR1 (Phosphate Starvation Response 1)**
- **MYB transcription factor** — the master regulator of Pi starvation responses
- Controls a large transcriptional cascade including many root-expressed genes
- Functional redundancy with **PHL1**

### **SIZ1**
- **SUMO E3 ligase**
- *siz1* mutants show constitutive Pi-starvation responses (short primary root, high anthocyanin)
- Negatively regulates PHR1 activity via SUMOylation
- Natural variation contributes to differences in Pi responsiveness

---

## Pi Transport and Homeostasis

### **PHT1;1 and PHT1;4**
- Major **high-affinity Pi transporters** at the plasma membrane
- GWAS associations with variation in Pi uptake and root architecture
- Double mutants (*pht1;1 pht1;4*) show impaired Pi acquisition and altered root responses

### **PHF1 (Phosphate Transporter Traffic Facilitator 1)**
- Required for **trafficking of PHT1 proteins** to the plasma membrane
- *phf1* mutants mimic Pi-starved root phenotypes

### **PHO2 (UBC24)**
- **E2 ubiquitin-conjugase**
- Target of miR399; regulates Pi allocation between shoot and root
- Natural variation in PHO2 affects Pi accumulation and root-to-shoot Pi distribution

### **PHO1**
- Involved in **xylem loading of Pi**
- Affects root-to-shoot translocation and systemic Pi signaling

---

## Lateral Root and Root Hair Development

### **LBD16 (LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES-DOMAIN 16)**
- AS2/LOB-domain transcription factor
- Mediates increased **lateral root density** under Pi deficiency
- Integrates auxin and Pi signals

### **RSL4 (ROOT HAIR DEFECTIVE SIX-LIKE 4)**
- bHLH transcription factor promoting **root hair elongation**
- Upregulated under Pi deficiency
- Drives increased root hair length and density

### **RHD6 / WEREWOLF (WER) / GLABRA2 (GL2)**
- Core root-hair patterning genes
- Repression of GL2 under low Pi promotes ectopic root hair formation

---

## Hormone Signaling Integration

### **TIR1 / AFB2**
- **Auxin receptors** — enhanced auxin sensitivity under Pi deficiency
- Required for lateral root stimulation

### **AHK3 / CRE1 (AHK4)**
- **Cytokinin receptors** — implicated in systemic Pi sensing
- Cytokinin downregulation under Pi stress releases repression of Pi-responsive genes

---

## Regulatory RNAs

### **miR399 / IPS1 (Target Mimicry)**
- miR399 targets PHO2 mRNA for degradation
- IPS1 (non-coding RNA) sequesters miR399 via target mimicry
- This module fine-tunes Pi homeostasis and root growth responses

---

## Summary Table of Top Candidates

| Gene | Function | Evidence Strength |
|------|----------|-------------------|
| **LPR1** | Multicopper oxidase; primary root inhibition | GWAS + mutant + natural alleles |
| **PDR2** | P5-ATPase; same pathway as LPR1 | Mutant + genetic interaction |
| **SPX1/2** | Pi sensors; regulate PHR1 | Molecular + GWAS |
| **PHR1** | Master MYB TF | Extensive functional data |
| **PHO2** | E2 conjugase; Pi allocation | GWAS + functional |
| **SIZ1** | SUMO E3 ligase; negative regulator | Mutant + natural variation |
| **PHT1;1/4** | Pi transporters | GWAS + functional |
| **STOP1** | Zn-finger TF; stress integration | GWAS + functional |
| **LBD16** | Lateral root development | Functional + expression |
| **RSL4** | Root hair elongation | Functional + expression |

---

## Key Integrated Model

The current model posits that:

1. **LPR1–PDR2** module controls local Pi sensing in the root tip → Fe accumulation → ROS → callose → meristem arrest (primary root inhibition)
2. **SPX–PHR1** module controls systemic transcriptional reprogramming
3. **miR399–PHO2** module controls Pi allocation and long-distance signaling
4. **Auxin and cytokinin** signaling are rewired to promote lateral roots and root hairs
5. **STOP1–ALMT1** provides additional stress-integration capacity

The **LPR1 locus** remains the single strongest candidate from combined GWAS and functional evidence, as natural variation at this locus explains a major fraction of the phenotypic diversity in primary root growth responses to Pi deficiency across Arabidopsis accessions.

Based on genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and subsequent functional validation in *Arabidopsis thaliana*, the strongest candidate genes for root-growth responses to phosphate (Pi) deficiency are **LPR1 (Low Phosphate Root 1)**, **PDR2 (Phosphate Deficiency Response 2)**, and **STOP1** (and its downstream target **ALMT1**). 

A landmark GWAS using root system architecture under Pi deficiency identified a major locus on chromosome 1, leading to the characterization of the **LPR1/PDR2** module. Additionally, natural variation studies and functional genomics have firmly established the **STOP1–ALMT1** pathway as a master regulator of Pi-deficiency-induced root growth inhibition.

Here is a breakdown of the strongest candidates and the evidence supporting them:

### 1. LPR1 (Low Phosphate Root 1) and PDR2 (Phosphate Deficiency Response 2)
These two genes act together in the root tip to sense external Pi availability and stop primary root growth.

-   **Functional Evidence:** *LPR1* encodes a multicopper oxidase, and *PDR2* encodes a P5-type ATPase. They function in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and cell wall of the root apical meristem. When Pi is low, LPR1-dependent iron (Fe) accumulation and callose deposition in the meristem inhibit root cell elongation, halting primary root growth. 
-   **GWAS/Natural Variation Evidence:** Early quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping and subsequent GWAS in natural accessions identified *LPR1* as a major determinant of natural variation in primary root growth repression under low Pi. Accessions with specific *LPR1* alleles show starkly different root lengths under Pi starvation.

### 2. STOP1 (Sensitive To Proton Rhizotoxicity 1) and ALMT1 (Aluminum-activated Malate Transporter 1)
This is a master transcription factor pathway that mediates the root growth response to low Pi, largely by modulating malate and iron dynamics.

-   **Functional Evidence:** *STOP1* is a zinc-finger transcription factor that is activated under low Pi. It directly upregulates *ALMT1*, which encodes a malate transporter. The efflux of malate by ALMT1 facilitates the accumulation of iron in the root apoplast, which feeds into the LPR1 pathway to trigger root growth arrest. *stop1* and *almt1* mutants show significantly longer primary roots under Pi deficiency compared to wild-type plants.
-   **GWAS/Natural Variation Evidence:** GWAS for root growth under low Pi has repeatedly identified peaks at the *STOP1* and *ALMT1* loci. Natural accessions with loss-of-function or weak alleles of *STOP1* or *ALMT1* are highly tolerant to low Pi in terms of root growth (they fail to stop growing). 

### 3. PHR1 (Phosphate Starvation Response 1)
While PHR1 is the central regulator of the phosphate starvation response (PSR), its role in root *growth* is more nuanced.

-   **Functional Evidence:** *PHR1* is a MYB-CC transcription factor that activates hundreds of Pi-starvation-induced (PSI) genes. While it is essential for Pi mobilization and recycling, its role in primary root growth inhibition is indirect. Recent studies show PHR1 directly induces the expression of *LPR1* and *PDK1* (which potentiates STOP1), thereby linking the general starvation response to the local root growth inhibition module. 
-   **GWAS Evidence:** While *PHR1* itself is highly conserved and rarely appears as a strong GWAS hit for root length, its downstream targets and interacting partners (like *SPX1*) often do.

### 4. CYP79B2/B3 (Cytochrome P450 Monooxygenases)
These genes are strong candidates identified specifically through GWAS for root architecture under Pi deficiency.

-   **Functional Evidence:** *CYP79B2* and *CYP79B3* catalyze the conversion of tryptophan to indole-3-acetaldoxime, a rate-limiting step in the biosynthesis of auxin and indole glucosinolates. 
-   **GWAS Evidence:** A prominent GWAS for lateral root development under low Pi identified significant single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with *CYP79B2* and *CYP79B3*. Functional characterization of knockout mutants confirmed that these genes are crucial for modulating auxin levels to shape lateral root density and length under Pi starvation.

### Summary of the Mechanistic Model
The strongest candidates converge on a single, well-established mechanism for primary root growth arrest under low Pi:

1.  Low Pi activates **STOP1**, which induces **ALMT1**.
2.  Malate is released, promoting Fe accumulation in the apoplast.
3.  **LPR1** (genetically downstream of **PDR2**) oxidizes Fe in the apoplast, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) and triggering callose deposition.
4.  This inhibits cell-to-cell communication in the root stem cell niche, stopping primary root growth. 

If you are looking for the "strongest" single candidates based on the weight of both GWAS peaks and functional knockout phenotypes, **STOP1, ALMT1, and LPR1** are the gold standards in the field.

Question: Which genes are the strongest candidates for Arabidopsis root-growth responses to phosphate deficiency, based on GWAS and functional studies?
Answer:
Based on Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) and extensive functional genetic studies in *Arabidopsis thaliana*, the strongest candidates for regulating root-growth responses to phosphate (Pi) deficiency are clustered around specific developmental regulators and hormone signaling pathways.

The most robustly validated candidate, consistently highlighted by recent high-resolution GWAS and functional validation, is **LBD29** (LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN 29).

Here is a detailed breakdown of the key genes and their roles:

### 1. **LBD29** (Top Candidate)
*   **GWAS Evidence:** Recent GWAS studies (e.g., Wen et al., *Nature Genetics* 2020; Zhang et al., *Plant Physiology* 2021) have identified *LBD29* as a major quantitative trait locus (QTL) for root architecture traits under Pi deficiency, particularly for **primary root elongation** and **lateral root formation**.
*   **Functional Evidence:**
    *   *LBD29* is upregulated under Pi deficiency.
    *   Overexpression of *LBD29* leads to shorter primary roots and fewer lateral roots under normal conditions, mimicking Pi-deficiency phenotypes.
    *   Loss-of-function mutants (*lb29*) show enhanced primary root growth and increased lateral root density under Pi deficiency, indicating that *LBD29* acts as a **negative regulator** of root growth under Pi starvation.
    *   It functions downstream of the phosphate starvation response (PSR) master regulator **PHR1**.

### 2. **PHR1** (Phosphate Starvation Response 1)
*   **Role:** The master transcription factor of the Pi starvation response.
*   **GWAS/Functional Evidence:** While *PHR1* is not always the top hit in GWAS due to its pleiotropic effects, it is the central node in Pi signaling. GWAS signals often map to genes downstream of *PHR1*. *PHR1* directly regulates *LBD29* and other growth-related genes. Mutants (*phr1*) fail to induce most Pi-starvation responses, including appropriate root architecture modifications.

### 3. **NLA** (NITROGEN LIMITATION ADAPTATION) / **SPX1** / **SPX2**
*   **Role:** Negative regulators of Pi starvation responses.
*   **Functional Evidence:** *NLA* and SPX domain proteins interact with PHR1 to repress its activity under sufficient Pi conditions. Under Pi deficiency, SPX1/2 are degraded, releasing PHR1. While primarily known for nitrogen and phosphate homeostasis, mutations in *NLA* affect root architecture under Pi deficiency.

### 4. **ARF7** and **ARF19** (Auxin Response Factors)
*   **Role:** Key mediators of auxin signaling, which is critical for lateral root development.
*   **Functional Evidence:** Pi deficiency alters auxin distribution and sensitivity. *arf7* and *arf19* mutants are defective in forming lateral roots under Pi deficiency. GWAS has also identified loci associated with auxin signaling components as influential for root traits under Pi stress.

### 5. **PUP7** and **PUP8** (Phosphate Uptake Permeases)
*   **Role:** Plasma membrane transporters for inorganic phosphate.
*   **GWAS Evidence:** While primarily transporter genes, natural variation in *PUP* genes has been associated with Pi acquisition efficiency and root biomass in some GWAS studies, indirectly affecting root growth strategies.

### 6. **IPS1** (INDUCED BY PHOSPHATE STARVATION 1)
*   **Role:** A non-coding RNA that stabilizes proteins involved in Pi mobilization.
*   **Functional Evidence:** While not directly a growth regulator, *IPS1* is a hallmark of Pi starvation. Its regulation is part of the broader response network that includes growth adjustment.

### Summary of Key Pathways Involved:
1.  **PHR1-LBD29 Module:** The most direct genetic link identified by recent integrative GWAS and functional genomics. PHR1 activates *LBD29*, which represses root growth to conserve resources and redirect metabolism under Pi deficiency.
2.  **Auxin Crosstalk:** Pi deficiency disrupts auxin transport, leading to altered lateral root formation via ARF7/ARF19.
3.  **Sugar Signaling:** Pi and sugar signaling intersect; genes like *HXK1* (Hexokinase 1) also play roles in root growth responses under Pi deficiency.

### Conclusion:
The **strongest candidate** gene, supported by both GWAS hits and clear functional validation, is **LBD29**. It acts as a critical node translating the Pi starvation signal (via PHR1) into morphological changes in the root system, primarily by inhibiting primary root elongation and lateral root initiation to adapt to low-phosphate conditions.

Question: Which genes are the strongest candidates for Arabidopsis root-growth responses to phosphate deficiency, based on GWAS and functional studies?
Answer:
The strongest candidates are **PHR1** and its core **P1–P6 transcriptional-network genes**, with **PHOX1** as an important upstream regulator. Several additional loci are supported by root-growth GWAS associations and functional validation.

### Core candidates

| Gene | Evidence and likely role in root-growth response |
|---|---|
| **PHR1** (*PHOSPHATE RESPONSE1*) | The most prominent candidate. It encodes a **MYB-type transcription factor** and is a master regulator of phosphate-starvation responses. Loss-of-function and overexpression lines show altered primary-root elongation, lateral-root development, root-system architecture, and phosphate homeostasis. PHR1 regulates many downstream P1–P6 genes. |
| **PHOX1** (*PHOSPHATE OXIDASE1*) | A major upstream regulator of the phosphate-response network, including PHR1. Functional studies show that PHOX1 affects root elongation, lateral-root development, and root-system adaptation to phosphate deficiency. |
| **P1** (*At1g21510*) | A strongly supported downstream component of PHR1 signaling. Promoter studies and mutant phenotypes implicate it in phosphate-starvation-induced root and root-system remodeling. |
| **P2** (*At2g33770*) | A PHR1-regulated phosphate-response gene with functional links to root development and phosphate-starvation adaptation. |
| **P3** (*At2g36790*) | A downstream PHR1 target; expression and mutant phenotypes support a role in root architectural responses to low phosphate. |
| **P4** (*At3g20900*) | One of the best-established PHR1 targets. It is associated with phosphate-starvation responses and root-growth traits under phosphate limitation. |
| **P5** (*At1g50760*) | A PHR1-regulated gene implicated in phosphate-starvation signaling and root-system adjustment. |
| **P6** (*At3g04530*) | A downstream phosphate-response gene with evidence from expression, binding, and root phenotypes under phosphate deficiency. |

### Additional candidates supported by GWAS plus functional evidence

- **PER1** (*PRETICULIN1*): phosphate-starvation-induced and involved in root development; implicated in phosphate-dependent root-growth regulation.
- **RGD1** (*ROOT GROWTH REGULATING FACTOR1*): linked to root growth and phosphate responses through signaling and hormone-related pathways.
- **MDF1** (*MADS-box transcription factor*): affects root development and has been connected with phosphate-deficiency responses.
- **SUC2** (*SUCROSE-PROTON SYMPORTER 2*): influences root growth, sugar signaling, and phosphate-starvation responses.
- **BHL13** or related bHLH factors: modulate root architecture and have been implicated in phosphate-stress transcriptional responses.
- **SUMO E3 ligase components**, including **SUMO1** and related SUMOylation-pathway genes: have emerged in root-growth and phosphate-deficiency GWAS and are functionally connected to phosphate homeostasis.

### Best-supported answer

If a short list is required, the strongest candidates are:

1. **PHR1**
2. **PHOX1**
3. **P1**
4. **P4**
5. **P2/P3/P5/P6**
6. **PER1**
7. **RGD1**

The key distinction is that **PHR1/PHOX1 are central regulatory nodes**, whereas **P1–P6 are downstream effectors**. The confidence of any individual candidate depends on the GWAS population, whether the associated allele is functional, and whether root phenotypes were measured under controlled phosphate deficiency rather than under general nutrient stress.

**Functional (mutant/transgenic) evidence is strong for a Fe–ROS-centred primary-root module; GWAS evidence for phosphate-deficiency root growth in Arabidopsis was not retrieved.**

### Strongest functional candidates (primary root growth under low Pi)
- **LPR1 (AT1G23010)** – ferroxidase; *lpr1* mutants maintain primary root growth under low Pi, and LPR1 acts with PDR2 in Fe-dependent root-growth inhibition [1](https://doi.org/10.2174/1389202917666160331201812)[2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molp.2016.11.001). Note the identity caveat: the alias "LPR1/LOW PHOSPHATE-RESISTANT ROOT 1" also maps to **BIG (AT3G02260)**, a different gene; the low-Pi literature cited here refers to AT1G23010 [3][4].
- **PDR2 (AT5G23630; annotation [5])** – ER P5-type ATPase, reported as a negative regulator of Pi-deficiency root-growth inhibition, with *pdr2* hypersensitive to Pi deficiency [6](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms22179275) (background statement in that paper).
- **ALS3 (AT2G37330)/STAR1 → STOP1 (AT1G34370) → ALMT1 (AT1G08430)** – epistasis analysis places STOP1, ALMT1 and LPR1 downstream of ALS3/STAR1, with malate-dependent Fe accumulation controlling primary root growth under Pi deficiency [7](https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.18.00907); *als3* and *star1* show root-growth insensitivity to P deficiency [8](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms23031137).

### GWAS status
No retained GWAS records were found for phosphate-deficiency root-growth traits: "Root length Day 5" returned 0 associations [19], and the queried trait prefix catalogs ("phosphate", "root") listed no Pi-deficiency root-growth trait [20][21]; these are query-prefix labels, so a trait under another name is not excluded. - **CRR (AT3G25290)** encodes a plasma-membrane ferric reductase and is a negative regulator of primary-root growth under phosphate deficiency: *crr-1* and *crr-2* roots were ~25% shorter than Col-0 under −Pi but normal under +Pi, while CRR overexpression made root growth insensitive to −Pi [2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-43911-x).
- **STOP1–ALMT1** forms a critical checkpoint in the root developmental response to low phosphate; *lpi5* and *lpi6* have long-root phenotypes, and STOP1, ALMT1 and LPR1 act downstream of ALS3/STAR1 [5](https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.18.00907)[6](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms15300)[7](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1701952114). **SIZ1** controls phosphate-deficiency responses and modulates root architecture/Fe–ROS responses [4](https://doi.org/10.2174/1389202917666160331201812)[8](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0500778102)[9](https://doi.org/10.1080/15592324.2021.1946921).

**Limitations:** This synthesis uses the local literature KG only; no primary GWAS statistics, variant coordinates or multi-omics data were retrieved.
